checks.claim: Key: a feature (body or plant part) that helps a living thing survive where it lives is an adaptation, and it is inherited
checks.note: 'a heritable trait that has been molded by natural selection to enhance the fitness of organisms in their environment'. National Geographic: 'An adaptation is passed from generation to generation' (https://education.nationalgeographic.org/resource/adaptation/).

checks.claim: Wrong: 'An instinct' (a behaviour an animal is born able to do, not a body part)
checks.note: 'an innate, complex pattern of behavior' that 'emerges without prior learning or experience'. Some instincts are behavioural adaptations, but the stem names body and plant parts (beak, shell, spines), so 'instinct' is not the name for 'a feature like this'.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'A habitat' (a place, not a body feature)
checks.note: 'the specific set of resources and environmental conditions in a given area that enable occupancy, survival, and reproduction'.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'A life cycle' (a series of stages)
checks.note: 'the complete sequence of developmental stages that an organism undergoes'.

checks.claim: Context: definitions of adaptation, instinct, habitat, life cycle
checks.note: All four as given match the sources at grade-5 level.

checks.claim: Key: a duckling inherits its webbed feet from its parents
checks.note: Webbing results from heritable changes in the genes for cell death between the toes: 'Different vertebrate species with webbed feet have different mutations that disrupt this process'.

checks.claim: Context: a duckling's webs take shape inside the egg, before it has ever swum
checks.note: Study of mallard embryos (Developmental mechanisms underlying webbed foot morphological diversity in waterbirds, 2020): at St. 35 'interdigital tissue remained between toes II and III, and toes III and IV'; 'After St. 36, when claws had already formed, interdigital tissues remained as webbing'. These are embryonic stages, well before hatching. Grokipedia Webbed foot: webbing persists when the interdigital cell death of embryogenesis is suppressed (https://grokipedia.com/page/Webbed_foot).

checks.claim: Wrong: 'Swimming stretches its toes into webs'
checks.note: The webbing is already present in the embryo; use cannot make it.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'It grows them because it wants to swim'
checks.note: Berkeley lists 'organisms trying to adapt' as a misconception: selection 'does not involve effort, trying, or wanting'.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'Cold pond water makes its toes grow webs'
checks.note: 'Individual organisms cannot adapt'; an individual's response to conditions is acclimation, which is not inherited (Grokipedia Adaptation: 'non-heritable adjustments within an individual's lifetime').

checks.claim: Context: no animal grows an adaptation by wanting it or using a body part; adaptations build up over many generations
checks.note: Acclimation and plasticity are 'not transmitted across generations'; 'small, heritable variations could accumulate gradually under selective pressures'.

checks.claim: Stem: 'Ducks, geese and other water birds have webbed feet'
checks.note: 'Palmate feet, common in ducks and geese'. Minor: not every water bird is web-footed (grebes and coots have lobed toes), but the stem reads as a generic of the group the question is about; optional polish 'Ducks, geese and many other water birds'.

checks.claim: Key: blubber plus dense fur suit icy polar seas
checks.note: Blubber's primary role is 'thermoregulation, acting as an effective insulator against conductive heat loss in cold water'; it allows 'survival in extreme polar environments'; thickness is greatest in polar and subpolar species.

checks.claim: Wrong: hot sandy deserts, steamy rainforests, dry grasslands
checks.note: Blubber is a marine-mammal insulator against frigid water; none of the three habitats is a cold sea, so none is defensible as best.

checks.claim: Context: seals and walruses keep warm in freezing water under thick blubber
checks.note: Walruses are named among pinnipeds that 'possess a thick subcutaneous blubber layer'; blubber typical of 'whales, seals, and walruses'.

checks.claim: Context: dense fur traps a layer of still air against the skin
checks.note: Fur insulates by 'trapping a layer of still air adjacent to the skin'.

checks.claim: Key: a sandy-brown lizard unseen on sand is camouflaged
checks.note: 'an antipredator adaptation in which animals and plants employ coloration' to be inconspicuous; 'Background matching aligns an organism's spectral reflectance and spatial patterns with the environment'. Grokipedia Crypsis: the tawny dragon lizard's patterns on 'sandy substrates' help it 'evade avian and reptilian predators' (https://grokipedia.com/page/Crypsis).

checks.claim: Wrong: 'Warning colours' (conspicuous, the reverse of hiding)
checks.note: Aposematism uses 'conspicuous warning signals, such as bright colors'; crypsis and aposematism are framed as a 'fundamental opposition'.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'Hibernation', 'Migration'
checks.note: Seasonal rest and seasonal travel; neither is colouring and neither explains a hawk looking straight at the lizard and missing it.

checks.claim: Context: warning colours, bright reds and yellows, tell hunters an animal is poisonous or stings
checks.note: Signals of 'toxins, venom'; bright reds, yellows, oranges; wasps' stripes signal stinging. Grade-level simplification (some warn of bad taste) is still true.

checks.claim: Key: a short, thick, cone-shaped beak is built for cracking hard seeds
checks.note: Finches have 'stout, conical beaks optimized for husking and crushing seeds'; Galapagos ground finches have 'robust, deep beaks for cracking large seeds'.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'Sipping nectar from flowers' (long, thin beaks)
checks.note: 'Hummingbirds' long, delicate beaks allow them to reach deep into flowers to drink their sweet nectar.' Grokipedia Hummingbird: 'elongated bills ... to match specific floral corollas'.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'Tearing meat from prey' (hooked beaks)
checks.note: Raptors have 'hooked, robust beaks to grasp and tear flesh'.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'Probing mud for worms' (long, slender bills)
checks.note: Shorebirds use 'long, slender bills to extract invertebrates from mud'.

checks.claim: Context: finches' stout cone beaks crush seeds; long thin beak for nectar; hooked beak tears meat; long slender bill probes mud
checks.note: All four pairings match the sources.

checks.claim: Key: wide, flat, ridged grinding back teeth and no long pointed front teeth mean a plant-eater (grass and leaves)
checks.note: Herbivores have 'broad, flat molars for grinding tough vegetation'; horses' 'flat, ridged molars'.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'Rabbits and mice' (a meat-eater's sharp canines and carnassials)
checks.note: Carnivores have 'sharp, pointed teeth for tearing flesh, such as canines and carnassials in mammals'.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'Fish and frogs' (pointed gripping teeth)
checks.note: Fish-eating hunters such as pike have conical, fang-like teeth for seizing slippery prey; otters and seals likewise have pointed teeth. Clearly not a skull of wide, ridged grinders.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'Beetles and ants'
checks.note: The best-known ant-eaters do NOT have sharp pointed teeth: the aardvark (diet over 90% ants and termites) has no incisors or canines (I 0/0, C 0/0) and only peg-like cheek teeth 'adapted for grinding'; the nine-banded armadillo eats mostly 'beetles, wasps, and ants' with 'simple peg-like teeth' (https://grokipedia.com/page/Armadillo); anteaters are 'toothless' (https://grokipedia.com/page/Anteater). An aardvark or armadillo skull would show 'no long, pointed teeth at the front'. The key still wins because those pegs are not wide and ridged, but an expert can object to 'ants'. Fix: 'Beetles and worms' (the prey of shrews, moles and hedgehogs, which do have sharp pointed teeth).

checks.claim: Context: 'Animals that eat other animals, from mice to fish to insects, have sharp, pointed teeth for gripping, tearing or piercing their prey.'
checks.note: Stated as a rule for all animal-eaters, it is false for insect-eaters: of ant- and termite-eating mammals, 'Most have reduced teeth'; anteaters and pangolins have none, the aardvark and armadillos have blunt peg teeth. Grokipedia Insectivore hedges with 'Many exhibit specialized dentition featuring sharp incisors and molars' (https://grokipedia.com/page/Insectivore). Fix: 'Hunters such as foxes, seals and shrews, which catch mice, fish and beetles, have sharp, pointed teeth for gripping, tearing or piercing their prey.' (and change the choice to 'Beetles and worms' to match).

checks.claim: Key: a cactus stores most of its water in its stem
checks.note: Stems hold water in thin-walled parenchyma, storing 'substantial volumes absorbed during rare precipitation events'; Grokipedia Xerophyte: in Opuntia and Cereus stem tissues hold 80-95% water.

checks.claim: Stem: a cactus can go months without rain and swells when rain comes
checks.note: Succulent stems 'endure droughts lasting years' (large saguaros reported to persist over two years without rain, weakly sourced); ribs allow 'reversible expansion and contraction'. 'Months' is safely within this.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'In its spines'
checks.note: Spines are modified leaves for defence and shade; they are not water stores.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'In its roots'
checks.note: A few cacti store water in large tuberous roots (Peniocereus greggii's tuber can top 40 lb; Felger and Henrickson: tuberous roots 'provide water and food-storing capacity'), but the stem's 'swells up when rain finally comes' points to the typical cactus, whose roots are shallow and fibrous. Not defensible as the answer for 'a cactus'.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'In its flowers'
checks.note: Flowers are short-lived reproductive parts, not water stores.

checks.claim: Context: pleats let the stem swell after rain and shrink in dry months
checks.note: Ribs or tubercles let the cortex expand and contract as hydration changes.

checks.claim: Context: spines are leaves of a special kind that guard it from animals
checks.note: Spines 'constitute modified leaves'; 'evolved primarily as a mechanical defense against herbivores'.

checks.claim: Context: its shallow roots spread wide to soak up rain quickly
checks.note: Most cacti have 'shallow, fibrous root systems that spread laterally near the soil surface', absorbing moisture from scattered rain quickly; a few (Lophophora, Ariocarpus) have taproots, so the generic holds.

checks.claim: Key: a deep desert taproot reaches water deep underground
checks.note: 'In arid regions, plants often develop roots exceeding 10 meters to reach groundwater'; deep taproots 'tap into groundwater during periods of surface drought'. Wikipedia Phreatophyte: deep-rooted plants such as mesquite take much of their water from the saturated zone (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phreatophyte).

checks.claim: Stem: some desert trees and shrubs send a root many metres down
checks.note: Oneseed juniper roots to 60 m; the record, Boscia albitrunca of the Kalahari, 68 m (1974). 'Many metres' is safe.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'Rain that has just fallen'
checks.note: Fresh rain is caught by shallow, laterally spreading roots near the surface; a deep root's job is groundwater, so the choice is wrong for 'a deep root like this'.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'Food stored deep in the soil'
checks.note: Roots 'absorb water and dissolved minerals'; the page never has them take up food. Plants make their food by photosynthesis (https://grokipedia.com/page/Photosynthesis).

checks.claim: Wrong: 'Warmth deep in the ground'
checks.note: Deep soil only has damped, lagged temperature swings ('transferred to sub surface layers but at reduced rates as depth increases'); in a hot desert the deep soil is cooler than the surface, and no source gives warmth as a reason for deep roots (Grokipedia Root names gravitropism and growth toward water, not toward warmth).

checks.claim: Context: deep roots reach water that stays far underground after the surface dries; other desert plants spread shallow roots for fresh rain
checks.note: Matches 'groundwater during periods of surface drought' and Grokipedia Cactus's shallow lateral roots.

checks.claim: Context: 'no root goes looking for food, because plants make their own food from sunlight'
checks.note: True of green plants, and the bank's how-plants-make-food unit already teaches that minerals are not food. Pedantic exceptions exist (root parasites such as broomrapes and the desert's sandfood take food from a host), so optional polish: 'no green plant's root goes looking for food'.

checks.claim: Key: dropping leaves saves water in the frozen months
checks.note: Deciduous plants lose leaves 'to conserve water or to better survive winter weather conditions' and can reduce water loss because liquid water is scarce on cold winter days. Grokipedia Deciduous: shedding helps 'prevent water loss through transpiration' (https://grokipedia.com/page/Deciduous). Other true reasons exist (frost injury to leaves, ice-storm breakage, energy), but none of them is offered as a wrong choice, so the key is the only defensible answer.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'They catch more sunlight on bare twigs'
checks.note: Leaves are the light-catching organs; a few hardwoods keep a little chlorophyll in twigs and buds (Penn State Extension, https://extension.psu.edu/silent-survivors-the-winter-life-of-trees), but bare twigs catch far less light than leaves, so 'more sunlight' is false.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'They make more food without leaves'
checks.note: In winter 'photosynthesis cannot produce energy as fast as respiration expends it'; dropping leaves shuts photosynthesis off, so the tree makes less food, not more.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'They grow taller while they are bare'
checks.note: Winter bud dormancy is 'the cessation of growth in apical and lateral buds'; growth resumes in spring. No height growth in winter.

checks.claim: Context: leaves let water escape into the air; in winter cold, frozen ground gives roots little water to replace it
checks.note: Water is 'often in short supply because of freezing'. Grokipedia Transpiration: stomata account for about 90-95% of water lost from leaves (https://grokipedia.com/page/Transpiration).

checks.claim: Context: leaves are where a tree makes its food, so a bare tree rests through winter until new leaves open in spring
checks.note: 'energy conservation during unfavorable seasons'; 'rapid regrowth of new foliage in spring'. Penn State notes trees are 'not completely dormant', but 'rests' is a true grade-level simplification.

unit_notes: One error, in the teeth question (e7b03bbb46): the context says every animal-eater, insect-eaters included, has sharp pointed teeth, and the wrong choice 'Beetles and ants' invites the famous ant-eaters (aardvark: no front teeth, peg-like grinding cheek teeth; armadillo: peg teeth; anteater and pangolin: no teeth). Suggested fix: choice 'Beetles and worms' and a context that names hunters (foxes, seals, shrews) rather than stating a rule for all animal-eaters. Checked as asked: duck webbing is present in mallard embryos from about HH stage 35-36, well before hatching, so 'inside the egg' holds; cactus stem as the main water store holds (a few tuber-rooted cacti such as Peniocereus are rare exceptions, not a problem for the stem's swelling cactus); 'Warmth deep in the ground' is wrong; the winter water-saving reason holds and no wrong choice is partly true; adaptations inherited, not gained in one lifetime, is supported by Grokipedia Adaptation, National Geographic and Berkeley.
